edge.title: The local number that isn't local
edge.anchor: Cyber Command seized illegal SIM boxes linked to online frauds from two Whitefield apartments in Bengaluru (Times of India, Deccan Herald, 22 Oct).
edge.setup: Your phone rings from an ordinary-looking Indian mobile number, even a Bengaluru-looking one. The caller sounds professional, quotes your bank or courier, and says your account or parcel has a problem that needs fixing on this call. Because the number looks local, you assume the call is real.
edge.tell: You are being asked to act on a call you did not start, and the number on your screen is the only proof of who it is.
move: Do not share an OTP, PIN, card number or app screen, whatever the caller already knows about you.
Hang up and call back on the number printed on your card, statement or the official app, never on the number that called you.
If money has already moved, report it at once on the national cyber crime helpline 1930 and tell your bank.
Treat urgency ('within 10 minutes') as part of the script, not a reason to hurry.
edge.why: A phone number used to be hard to fake, so it worked as proof of identity. Equipment like a SIM box lets a caller located anywhere present as an ordinary local mobile number, so the number now proves nothing. What a fraudster cannot fake is you initiating the contact through a channel you already trust. Calling back on a number you looked up yourself restores that.
edge.variants: Same shape: a 'delivery agent' texting from a mobile number, a 'KYC update' call from a landline-looking number, a 'relative in trouble' call from an unknown local number.

lens.name: Costly signals
lens.one_line: A signal is only trustworthy if it is expensive for a liar to fake.
lens.detail: We rely on cheap markers of trust: a local phone number, a logo, a polished video, a confident tone. They work only while faking them costs more than the fraud earns. When technology makes a marker cheap to copy, it stops carrying information, and you must switch to something the faker cannot produce cheaply.
elsewhere: A letterhead or PDF 'offer letter' versus a verified company email domain.
A five-star review count versus a reviewer with a long, varied history.
A flat shown in a video versus a key that turns in the lock.
lens.test: What would this signal cost a liar to fake? If almost nothing, treat it as no evidence.
lens.today: Cyber Command seized SIM boxes from two Whitefield apartments that were linked to online frauds (Times of India, Deccan Herald). A Bengaluru-looking mobile number used to be a cheap-to-check signal of a real local caller; with such equipment it costs a fraudster little, so it no longer tells you who is calling.

moved.what: Cyber Command seized illegal SIM boxes from two Whitefield apartments, linked to online frauds (Times of India, Deccan Herald).
moved.so_what: A local-looking mobile number is no proof of a real caller; for any bank or courier call, hang up and call back on the number on your card or app.

carry_over.prompt: A shocking clip of a blast at a landmark lands in your family group with a caption urging everyone to share it fast: what is the tell?
carry_over.answer: A shocking clip with no named source, no outlet reporting it, and a caption telling you to spread it fast.
